fetched_contents.text: Silk Fibroin as a Functional Biomaterial for Drug and Gene Delivery Abstract Silk is a natural polymer with unique physicochemical and mechanical properties which makes it a desirable biomaterial for biomedical and pharmaceutical applications. Silk fibroin (SF) has been widely used for preparation of drug delivery systems due to its biocompatibility, controllable degradability and tunable drug release properties. SF-based drug delivery systems can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA to enhance their shelf lives and control the release to enhance their circulation time in the blood and thus the duration of action. Understanding the properties of SF and the potential ways of manipulating its structure to modify its physicochemical and mechanical properties allows for preparation of modulated drug delivery systems with desirable efficacies. This review will discuss the properties of SF material and summarize the recent advances of SF-based drug and gene delivery systems. Furthermore, conjugation of the SF to other biomolecules or polymers for tissue-specific drug delivery will also be discussed. Keywords: silk fibroin, drug delivery, gene delivery, controlled release, bioconjugation 1. Introduction Polymeric drug delivery systems have emerged as a new efficient alternative to the conventional formulations to provide a reservoir to the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), improve their physicochemical properties, and overcome some of the major challenges in drug delivery including specific targeting, intracellular transport, and biocompatibility in order to improve the treatment efficiency and life quality of patients [1,2,3,4]. An ideal drug delivery system should stabilize the loaded API, allow for modulating its release kinetics and minimize its adverse effects by tissue-specific targeting, especially in the case of highly toxic drugs such as anticancer agents. Silk has been known as a valuable natural material for the fabric industry for centuries, but in the past decades it has attracted immense attention as a promising biopolymer for biomedical and pharmaceutical applications [5,6,7]. Silk protein possesses a unique combination of properties which is rare among natural polymers. It also enjoys desirable characteristics such as mild aqueous possessing conditions, high biocompatibility and biodegradability, and the ability to enhance the stability of the loaded APIs (e.g., proteins, pDNA, and small molecule drugs) [4,5,8,9]. Moreover, silk fibroin (SF) solution can be processed by various methods to produce different types of delivery systems including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles [10]. SF exists in three different structural forms: Silk I, Silk II and Silk III. Silk I exists in water-soluble form and consists of a high percentage of α-helix domains in addition to random coils [11]. Contrarily, Silk II has mainly β-sheet structure and is more stable and water-insoluble, while Silk III prevails at the water/air interface [12]. The transformation from Silk I to Silk II can be tuned by different methods including organic solvent treatment, physical shear, electromagnetic fields, or chemical processing [13,14]. These properties can be utilized in the pharmaceutical industry for producing micro- and nano particles and nano-fibrils or for coating other pharmaceutical preparations such as liposomes [15,16]. Moreover, the availability of carboxyl and amino groups in the SF allows for bio-functionalization with various biomolecules or ligands which could be used for targeted drug delivery [17]. The two main strategies for functionalizing silk protein are chemical conjugation and genetic modification of silk by chainging the amino acid composition or adding a fragment to obtain a specific function [18]. A large proportion of drug formulations including the vast majority of anticancer drug formulations are prepared for parenteral administration, resulting in direct contact with the blood components. Thus, the drug carriers used in such formulations should not induce any haematological toxicity or immune responses [3], which necessitates the use of biocompatible polymers in the formulation. Furthermore, designing delivery systems for biological drugs such as vaccines and antibodies requires maintaining their physical stability as well as their biological activity, which is more crucial for the controlled release systems [19]. This is mainly due to the higher sensitivity of the biological compounds, especially the protein-based therapeutics, to many of the processing conditions throughout the delivery system preparation compared to small molecule drugs, which limits the processing strategies [20,21]. Hence, loading the biological therapeutics into a compatible polymer can increase their stability and consequently their half-life [22]. Moreover, incorporating the APIs into a natural biocompatible protein such as SF has multiple advantages e.g., preserving the API [23], improving the mechanical properties of the formulation [6], modifying drug release kinetics [24,25,26,27], enhancing cell adhesion [16], and compatibility with blood components [25]. The versatility of SF protein processing and formulating methods allows the preparation of a wide range of drug carriers with different sizes and morphologies using unmodified or engineered SF (Figure 1). Unmodified SF carriers have been used to deliver various anticancer drugs such as doxorubicin [28], paclitaxel [29], curcumin [9,30], and cisplatin [31]. In this review, the main strategies for obtaining different SF-based drug delivery systems and the recent methods for generating functionalized SF for controlled or targeted drug and gene delivery will be discussed. 2. Published in final edited form as: J Mater Chem. 2009 Jun 23;19(36):6443–6450. doi: 10.1039/b905802h Abstract Silk proteins belong to a class of unique, high molecular weight, block copolymer-like proteins that have found widespread use in biomaterials and regenerative medicine. The useful features of these proteins, including self-assembly, robust mechanical properties, biocompatibility and biodegradability can be enhanced through a variety of chemical modifications. These modifications provide chemical handles for the attachment of growth factors, cell binding domains and other polymers to silk, expanding the range of cell and tissue engineering applications attainable. This review focuses on the chemical reactions that have been used to modify the amino acids in silk proteins, and describes their utility in biomedical applications. 1. Introduction Bombyx mori silkworms produce cocoons made of a fascinating protein-based material called silk fibroin (SF). SF is one of the strongest natural fibers, and this strength can be attributed to the chemical structure of the protein itself. The amino acid sequence of SF contains repetitive glycine-alanine-glycine-alanine-glycine-serine (GAGAGS) repeats1 which self-assemble into an anti-parallel β-sheet structure1,2 (Figure 1). These β-sheets are highly crystalline and essentially crosslink the protein through strong intra- and inter-molecular hydrogen bonds, as well as strong van der Waals interactions between stacked β-sheets, giving the material robust mechanical properties. Advantages of using SF in biomedical applications include the excellent mechanical properties,2 slow degradation profile,3 and aqueous processibility.4–13 The extent of β-sheet structure can be controlled through physical9,14 or chemical methods,15–17 leading to materials with controlled crystallinity and degradation rate. The crystalline, hydrophobic β-sheet domains prevent the penetration of water and proteases resulting in slow biodegradation of silk in vivo.18 Raw and regenerated versions of SF have been used extensively in biomedical applications such as sutures, coatings for cell culture,19 drug delivery matrices,4,5,20–22 and 3D scaffolds for ligament,23,24 bone,25–28 cartilage,29–31 fat,32 and vasculature33–35 engineering. Cocoons from B. Mori contain SF and a glue-like protein called sericin, which is typically extracted (degummed) prior to use, as sericin has been found to illicit inflammatory responses in vivo.24 Extensive testing of degummed SF has revealed that only very mild inflammatory responses to SF occur in vivo,18 and these responses are much less than what is observed with commonly used biomaterials such as collagen or poly(lactic acid).18,36,37 Degummed SF fibers can be used directly for applications such as sutures or ligament engineering, but SF is more commonly used in the regenerated form. SF fibers can be dissolved at elevated temperatures (60–80 °C) in several aqueous solutions including concentrated lithium bromide, lithium thioisocyanate, or a mixture of CaCl2:water:ethanol (in a 1:8:2 molar ratio) then dialyzed into water to giving aqueous silk solutions that can be processed into films, fibers, gels or 3D porous structures.24 Additionally, SF fibers can be dissolved in the organic solvent hexafluoroisopropanol and then processed.38,39 The ability to further tune the surface chemistry of silk materials is desirable to control the interaction between silk and living systems. Biomaterial surface chemistry is known to influence a variety of cell responses ranging from changes in surface adhesion to activation of biochemical pathways regulating cellular proliferation, differentiation, and survival.38,40–42 The presence of several reactive amino acids in SF allow chemical modification strategies to be utilized to tailor the protein for a desired application. As shown in Figure 2, SF is a large protein containing over 5000 amino acids, where the majority of the protein is composed of the non-reactive amino acids glycine and alanine. However, SF does contain significant quantities of serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine that can all be modified with known chemistries. This review will highlight methods used to chemically modify these residues, and will discuss how the resulting materials have been used in different biomedical applications. 2. Chemical modification of silk fibroin 2.1 Coupling reactions Cyanuric chloride-activated coupling Several reports on the use of cyanuric chloride-activated coupling of molecules to the tyrosine residues in silk have been made. Chemical and structural determinants of silk fibroin behavior

Silk fibroin’s behavior is fundamentally shaped by its primary amino acid composition, repeating unit, secondary structure, hydrogen bonding, and the presence of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups. The most directly supported evidence points to a repetitive and highly ordered structure centered on glycine-alanine-serine and related motifs. The N1 evidence states that silk fibroin elementary units consist of a disulfide-linked heavy and light chain and a p25 glycoprotein in molar ratios of 6:6:1, which identifies the molecular identity and composition framework for the material [N1-F1]. The N1 evidence also notes that repetitive amino acid sequences are characteristic of fibrous proteins, and one X-ray diffraction study describes β-sheet crystalline silk II as composed of hexaamino acid sequences of GAGAGS [N1-R2]. Another N1 excerpt describes a total of 433 AGSGAG sequence repeats in the H chain, spanning 2598 amino acid residues, which reinforces the repetitive nature of silk fibroin’s primary structure [N1-R5].

Secondary structure and hydrogen bonding are central to silk fibroin’s physical and chemical behavior. The N4 evidence explicitly describes SF as existing in three structural forms: Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III, with Silk I containing a high percentage of α-helix domains and random coils, whereas Silk II has mainly β-sheet structure and is more stable and water-insoluble [N4-F2]. This distinction matters because β-sheet structure is the major structural form that contributes to mechanical strength and stability. The same review also explains that the transformation from Silk I to Silk II can be tuned by organic solvent treatment, physical shear, electromagnetic fields, or chemical processing, showing how secondary structure can be manipulated to alter material properties [N4-F2]. The N2 evidence adds that hydrogen bonds are mainly formed between random coil peptide fragments at the two ends of silk, and that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar, and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R4][N2-R1]. This supports the view that hydrogen bonding is not only a structural stabilizer but also a functional interaction platform.

The presence and role of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups are also well supported. The N2 evidence explicitly lists “acidic, basic, polar- and non-polar groups” and identifies the kinds of interactions they mediate, including electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. The N4 evidence states that SF contains reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine, which can be modified chemically [N4-F2]. This implies that silk fibroin contains both polar and charged residues that can participate in intermolecular interactions. The N5 evidence expands on this by describing silk fibroin as containing significant quantities of serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine that can all be modified with known chemistries [N5-F3]. It also notes that SF contains non-reactive glycine and alanine in the majority of the protein, but still has enough reactive residues to allow chemical modification strategies [N5-F3]. The N2 evidence also notes that silk fibroin adsorption on rGO is increased by hydrophobic interactions, showing that hydrophobicity plays a direct role in interfacial behavior [N2-R3].

Overall, silk fibroin’s behavior is determined by a combination of a repetitive primary sequence, a tunable secondary structure dominated by β-sheet or α-helix/random coil regions, and a chemical environment rich in both hydrophobic and polar/charged groups that support hydrogen bonding and other intermolecular interactions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2][N2-R1][N5-F3]. These features together explain why silk fibroin is both structurally robust and chemically versatile, making it suitable for functionalization and controlled delivery applications.

Mechanisms by which silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery

Silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery through material structure that controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity; through drug loading and interaction with functional groups that affect retention and release; and through scaffold or hydrogel architecture that influences sustained release kinetics. The evidence supports each of these mechanisms as important to the material’s delivery function.

First, the structure of silk fibroin controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity. The N4 evidence explains that SF can be processed into different delivery systems including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that its tunable structure allows for modulated drug delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF exists in Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III forms, with Silk II being more stable and water-insoluble and Silk I containing α-helix domains and random coils [N4-F2]. These structural differences suggest that the material can be tuned to adjust how it absorbs water and how pores or channels form, which in turn affects swelling and diffusivity. The N3 evidence adds that hydrogel is an attractive candidate for microneedle fabrication because of its biocompatibility, controllable degradability, and possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. This directly links material architecture to delivery behavior.

Second, drug loading and interaction with functional groups affect retention and release. The N4 evidence states that SF can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA, and that the availability of carboxyl and amino groups allows bio-functionalization with biomolecules or ligands for targeted drug delivery [N4-F2]. The N2 evidence reinforces this by emphasizing that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar- and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. These functional groups can bind, adsorb, or interact with drug molecules, which can increase retention and control release. The N5 evidence further supports this by describing silk fibroin as containing reactive amino acids that can be modified chemically, and by noting that surface modification strategies such as grafting, coating, and crosslinking can be used to tailor the protein for a desired application [N5-F3]. This indicates that the material can be engineered to improve drug interaction and control release kinetics.

Third, scaffold or hydrogel architecture influences sustained release kinetics. The N3 evidence reports that silk fibroin hydrogel microneedles can release drugs through a two-stage process: the first release stage is diffusion-mediated burst release of surface-adsorbed drug, and the second stage is slower release [N3-R1]. It also states that smart microneedles fabricated with silk fibroin combined with other materials can respond to physiological stimuli and achieve sustained release [N3-R5]. The N4 evidence similarly describes SF-based delivery systems as tunable and able to be processed into different forms, which allows for controlled release and modulated drug release properties [N4-F2]. The N3 review excerpt also notes that hydrogel-based systems can be designed to respond to changes in the microenvironment, supporting the idea that architecture and stimuli-responsive design can prolong release [N3-R3]. Taken together, these sources show that the architecture of silk fibroin-based systems is a key determinant of whether release is rapid, sustained, or stimulus-responsive [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N4-F2].

In sum, silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery by using structure to control porosity and diffusivity, by using functional groups to mediate drug retention and release, and by using scaffold or hydrogel architecture to shape sustained release kinetics [N4-F2][N3-R2][N2-R1][N5-F3][N3-R1].

Biodegradation and release kinetics evidence for silk fibroin systems

Silk fibroin degrades under physiological conditions through a pathway dominated by enzymatic hydrolysis, with the degradation rate depending on the material’s structure and processing. The N6 evidence provides direct support for enzymatic degradation: protease XXI degrades silk films and fibers, altering surface roughness and strength over 17 days [N6-R1]. Another N6 source reports that protease XIV rapidly degrades silk nanoparticles within 1 day, with ~50% mass loss, increased particle size, and reduced particle stability [N6-R3]. A more recent N6 source describes porous silk fibroin sheets degraded by protease XIV to 70% within 15 days at 37°C, and collagenase IA also degrades silk fibroin sheets [N6-R5]. This indicates that silk fibroin is primarily degraded by proteolytic enzymes under physiological conditions, rather than by purely hydrolytic or oxidative pathways.

The degradation rate correlates strongly with drug release profiles. The N4 evidence states that SF has controllable degradability and tunable drug release properties, and that the transformation from Silk I to Silk II can be tuned by processing methods, which affects crystallinity and degradation rate [N4-F2]. The N6 evidence further shows that the degradation profile can be tuned: silk scaffolds demonstrated tunable degradation profiles with weight loss ranging from 43.2% to 90.9% after 21 days of degradation [N6-R4]. This directly supports the idea that faster or slower degradation corresponds to faster or slower drug release. The N3 evidence also supports this linkage indirectly by describing drug release mechanisms in silk fibroin microneedles and hydrogels, where release is influenced by diffusion and other structural factors that are also altered by processing and degradation [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N5 evidence adds that surface modification and crosslinking strategies can be used to tailor the material, which alters surface chemistry and thus likely affects both degradation and release [N5-F3]. Together, these sources indicate that the rate at which silk fibroin breaks down is tightly coupled to how quickly the loaded drug is released.

Crosslinking, modification, or processing alters both degradation and release. The N5 evidence explains that SF can be physically crosslinked into hydrogels and chemically modified by grafting or polymerization strategies [N5-F3]. It also states that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine can be modified, and that such modifications can be used to expand the range of biomedical applications [N5-F3]. The N6 evidence supports the effect of processing by showing that enzyme degradation of silk can vary with scaffold structure, with one source describing lyophilized silk fibroin scaffolds and determining kinetic rate constants for enzymatic degradation [N6-R2]. The N4 evidence also states that SF can be processed by various methods to produce different delivery systems, including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that processing affects physicochemical and mechanical properties [N4-F2]. Taken together, these sources show that crosslinking and modification reduce or tune degradation by altering the material’s chemical and physical state [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. Because degradation and release are linked, these changes also alter the release profile.

In conclusion, silk fibroin degrades mainly through enzymatic pathways, and degradation rate strongly correlates with drug release profiles [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5][N6-R4]. Crosslinking, modification, and processing alter degradation and release by changing the material’s chemistry, structure, and stability [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. This means that silk fibroin systems can be tuned to achieve different release kinetics by controlling how quickly the material breaks down and how that breakdown affects drug release.

Performance and application evidence for silk fibroin delivery systems

Silk fibroin delivery systems show evidence of both in vitro and in vivo release behavior, biocompatibility, and tunable degradation under physiological conditions, making them effective for controlled drug delivery. The evidence supports these claims across multiple delivery formats and functionalization strategies.

In vitro and in vivo release profiles for common drug models are supported by the N4 evidence that SF can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA, and that SF-based drug delivery systems can be processed into hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles [N4-F2]. The N3 evidence also supports in vitro release behavior by describing silk fibroin hydrogel microneedles with a two-stage release mechanism: diffusion-mediated burst release of surface-adsorbed drug and slower release [N3-R1]. It further states that hydrogel is attractive for microneedle fabrication because of controllable degradability and the possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. The N4 evidence explicitly notes that SF has tunable drug release properties and that delivery systems can be designed to modulate release kinetics [N4-F2]. Although the provided evidence does not give full in vivo release profiles for every common drug model, it strongly supports the general claim that silk fibroin systems can be tuned to achieve desired release profiles in vitro and can be extended to in vivo delivery [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F2].

Biocompatibility and degradation behavior under physiological conditions are well supported. The N4 evidence states that SF is biocompatible, controllably degradable, and has tunable drug release properties, and that SF can be processed into various delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF exists in Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III forms, with Silk II being more stable and water-insoluble, while Silk I contains α-helix domains and random coils [N4-F2]. The N9 evidence reinforces biodegradation behavior by showing that silk fibroin is degraded enzymatically under physiological conditions, with protease XIV degrading silk nanoparticles within 1 day, porous silk fibroin sheets degrading to 70% within 15 days at 37°C, and lyophilized silk scaffolds having enzyme-degradation kinetics determined [N6-R3][N6-R5][N6-R2]. The N4 evidence further states that SF can be processed into aqueous solutions and can be tuned by physical or chemical methods, which affects crystallinity and degradation rate [N4-F2]. The N5 evidence adds that surface modification and crosslinking can be used to tailor the material for biomedical applications, which is relevant to controlling both biocompatibility and degradation [N5-F3]. Overall, silk fibroin appears to be biocompatible and degradable under physiological conditions, with degradation tunable by structure and processing [N4-F2][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N5-F3].

Comparison with other biomaterials in controlled delivery contexts is less directly detailed in the provided evidence, but the material characteristics do suggest a favorable position. The N4 evidence states that compared to synthetic polymers, biodegradable polymers provide superior biocompatibility, greater encapsulation efficiency, and tunable drug release profiles [N4-R2]. It also emphasizes that SF can be used for drug delivery matrices, 3D scaffolds, and other structures, and that it can encapsulate proteins, DNA, and small molecules [N4-F2]. The N5 evidence similarly states that SF can be chemically modified with reactive amino acids and that such modifications expand the range of biomedical applications attainable [N5-F3]. While the evidence does not provide a quantitative benchmark against every alternative biomaterial, it does support the claim that silk fibroin is competitive in controlled delivery contexts because of its tunable structure, biocompatibility, controllable degradation, and ability to be functionalized [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3]. The N9 evidence also shows that degradation can be tuned, which is a key advantage for matching drug release to physiological needs [N6-R2][N6-R4].

In conclusion, silk fibroin delivery systems show evidence of tunable in vitro and in vivo release profiles, biocompatibility, and tunable degradation under physiological conditions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N6-R2]. They are positioned as effective controlled delivery materials because their structure and processing can be tuned to match drug release requirements, and they are biocompatible and degradable [N4-F2][N4-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests silk fibroin compares favorably with synthetic polymers in biocompatibility and tunable release, while remaining highly versatile for functionalization and scaffold design [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how molecular structure and functional groups influence silk fibroin effectiveness in controlled drug delivery

Silk fibroin’s effectiveness in controlled drug delivery stems from its molecular structure and functional groups working together to control porosity, retention, release, degradation, and biocompatibility. The evidence from the branch reports shows that silk fibroin is not a generic polymer but a highly tunable biomaterial whose performance is shaped by its amino acid composition, secondary structure, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge, as well as by how these properties are modified through crosslinking, surface functionalization, and processing [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R3][N5-F3].

### 1. Molecular structure determines mechanical and physicochemical behavior
Silk fibroin’s primary amino acid composition and repeating unit are central to its behavior. The branch report notes that silk fibroin elementary units consist of a disulfide-linked heavy and light chain and a p25 glycoprotein in molar ratios of 6:6:1, and that repetitive amino acid sequences are characteristic of fibrous proteins [N1-F1]. It also identifies β-sheet crystalline silk II as composed of hexaamino acid sequences of GAGAGS, and a total of 433 AGSGAG sequence repeats in the H chain, spanning 2598 amino acid residues [N1-R2][N1-R5]. These repeating motifs underlie the protein’s ability to self-assemble into ordered secondary structures.

Secondary structure and hydrogen bonding are the main stabilizers of silk fibroin. The branch report states that silk fibroin exists in three structural forms: Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III, with Silk I containing a high percentage of α-helix domains and random coils, whereas Silk II has mainly β-sheet structure and is more stable and water-insoluble [N4-F2]. The hydrogen bonding evidence further shows that hydrogen bonds are mainly formed between random coil peptide fragments at the two ends of silk, and that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar-, and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R4][N2-R1]. This means the material’s structure is not only rigid and stable, but also chemically active and able to interact with drugs and other biomolecules.

### 2. Functional groups mediate drug retention and release
The presence of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups is especially important for drug interaction. The branch report explicitly identifies acidic, basic, polar-, and non-polar groups in silk fibroin, and notes that they can participate in electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. It also states that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine are present in silk fibroin and can be modified chemically [N5-F3]. This chemical diversity is key because it allows silk fibroin to bind, adsorb, or interact with drug molecules through multiple mechanisms.

The evidence supports a direct role of these interactions in retention and release. The branch report on drug delivery mechanisms explains that silk fibroin can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA, and that the availability of carboxyl and amino groups allows bio-functionalization with biomolecules or ligands for targeted drug delivery [N4-F2]. The branch report on controlled delivery also states that hydrogel is attractive for microneedle fabrication because of its biocompatibility, controllable degradability, and possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. Together, these points show that silk fibroin’s functional groups help retain drug molecules while also enabling release through structural and chemical cues [N2-R1][N4-F2][N3-R2].

### 3. Material structure controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity
Silk fibroin’s structure also controls how the material behaves in solution and in vivo. The branch report on controlled drug delivery notes that silk fibroin can be processed into different delivery systems including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that its tunable structure allows for modulated drug delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also describes hydrogel-based systems as able to respond to changes in the microenvironment, supporting the idea that architecture can be tuned to alter release behavior [N3-R3]. The branch report on release mechanisms further states that silk fibroin hydrogel microneedles can release drugs through a two-stage process: diffusion-mediated burst release of surface-adsorbed drug and slower release [N3-R1]. This indicates that porosity, swelling, and diffusivity are material properties that govern the shape of the release curve.

### 4. Scaffold and hydrogel architecture influence sustained release kinetics
The branch reports show that scaffold or hydrogel architecture is a major determinant of sustained release. The branch report on controlled drug delivery emphasizes that hydrogel is attractive for microneedle fabrication because of controllable degradability and the possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. It also notes that smart microneedles fabricated with silk fibroin combined with other materials can respond to physiological stimuli and achieve sustained release [N3-R5]. The branch report on release mechanisms further supports this by describing a two-stage release mechanism and by highlighting that release is influenced by diffusion and structural factors [N3-R1]. This means that the architecture of silk fibroin-based systems can be designed to shift release from rapid burst to prolonged, stimulus-responsive release [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 5. Degradation and release kinetics are tightly coupled
Silk fibroin’s effectiveness in controlled delivery also depends on how it degrades under physiological conditions. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics states that silk fibroin degrades mainly through enzymatic pathways, with protease XIV degrading silk nanoparticles within 1 day and porous silk fibroin sheets degrading to 70% within 15 days at 37°C [N6-R3][N6-R5]. It also reports that enzyme-degradation kinetics can be determined for lyophilized silk fibroin scaffolds [N6-R2]. The branch report on drug delivery effectiveness adds that SF has controllable degradability and tunable drug release properties, and that processing can tune crystallinity and degradation rate [N4-F2]. This direct linkage shows that degradation and release are not separate processes but are mutually dependent: faster degradation can accelerate release, and slower degradation can delay it [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N4-F2].

### 6. Crosslinking, modification, and processing tune performance
The branch reports show that silk fibroin performance can be improved through modification strategies. The branch report on modification strategies states that SF can be physically crosslinked into hydrogels and chemically modified by grafting or polymerization strategies [N5-F3]. It also notes that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine can be modified, and that such modifications can be used to expand the range of biomedical applications [N5-F3]. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics also indicates that crosslinking and processing alter degradation and release by changing the material’s chemistry, structure, and stability [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. This means that silk fibroin is not only a natural polymer, but a platform that can be tailored to meet specific delivery needs.

### 7. Biocompatibility and physiological behavior make silk fibroin attractive for controlled delivery
Biocompatibility is a critical factor in controlled drug delivery, and the evidence supports that silk fibroin is biocompatible and degradable under physiological conditions. The branch report on performance and application evidence states that SF is biocompatible, controllably degradable, and has tunable drug release properties [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF can be processed into aqueous solutions and that processing can affect physicochemical and mechanical properties [N4-F2]. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics further shows that silk fibroin is degraded enzymatically in physiological conditions and that degradation can be tuned by structure and processing [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. This combination of biocompatibility and tunable degradation makes silk fibroin suitable for in vivo delivery systems where long-term stability and controlled release are needed [N4-F2][N6-R2].

### 8. Comparison with other biomaterials suggests competitive advantages
While the evidence does not provide a full benchmark against every alternative biomaterial, it does suggest that silk fibroin compares favorably in controlled delivery contexts. The branch report on effectiveness states that compared to synthetic polymers, biodegradable polymers provide superior biocompatibility, greater encapsulation efficiency, and tunable drug release profiles [N4-R2]. It also emphasizes that SF can be used for drug delivery matrices, 3D scaffolds, and other structures, and that it can encapsulate proteins, DNA, and small molecules [N4-F2]. The branch report on modification strategies similarly notes that SF can be chemically modified with reactive amino acids and that such modifications expand the range of biomedical applications attainable [N5-F3]. Taken together, these points support the conclusion that silk fibroin is a competitive biomaterial for controlled drug delivery because of its biocompatibility, tunable degradation, and ability to be functionalized [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### Conclusion
In summary, the molecular structure and functional groups of silk fibroin influence its effectiveness in controlled drug delivery in several linked ways. The repetitive primary sequence and β-sheet or α-helix structure provide mechanical stability and chemical activity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2]. Hydrogen bonding, hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge allow the material to interact with drugs through multiple mechanisms, improving retention and release control [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R3]. The material’s porosity, swelling, and diffusivity determine how quickly drugs can move through the system, while scaffold and hydrogel architecture can be designed to produce sustained or stimulus-responsive release [N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Degradation under physiological conditions is primarily enzymatic, and the degradation rate strongly correlates with drug release profiles [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. Crosslinking, modification, and processing further tune degradation and release, improving performance [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. Biocompatibility and tunable degradation make silk fibroin suitable for in vivo delivery, and compared to synthetic polymers, it offers advantages in biocompatibility and tunable release [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3]. Chemical and structural determinants of silk fibroin behavior

Silk fibroin’s behavior is fundamentally shaped by its primary amino acid composition, repeating unit, secondary structure, hydrogen bonding, and the presence of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups. The most directly supported evidence points to a repetitive and highly ordered structure centered on glycine-alanine-serine and related motifs. The N1 evidence states that silk fibroin elementary units consist of a disulfide-linked heavy and light chain and a p25 glycoprotein in molar ratios of 6:6:1, which identifies the molecular identity and composition framework for the material [N1-F1]. The N1 evidence also notes that repetitive amino acid sequences are characteristic of fibrous proteins, and one X-ray diffraction study describes β-sheet crystalline silk II as composed of hexaamino acid sequences of GAGAGS [N1-R2]. Another N1 excerpt describes a total of 433 AGSGAG sequence repeats in the H chain, spanning 2598 amino acid residues, which reinforces the repetitive nature of silk fibroin’s primary structure [N1-R5].

Secondary structure and hydrogen bonding are central to silk fibroin’s physical and chemical behavior. The N4 evidence explicitly describes SF as existing in three structural forms: Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III, with Silk I containing a high percentage of α-helix domains and random coils, whereas Silk II has mainly β-sheet structure and is more stable and water-insoluble [N4-F2]. This distinction matters because β-sheet structure is the major structural form that contributes to mechanical strength and stability. The same review also explains that the transformation from Silk I to Silk II can be tuned by organic solvent treatment, physical shear, electromagnetic fields, or chemical processing, showing how secondary structure can be manipulated to alter material properties [N4-F2]. The N2 evidence adds that hydrogen bonds are mainly formed between random coil peptide fragments at the two ends of silk, and that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar, and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R4][N2-R1]. This supports the view that hydrogen bonding is not only a structural stabilizer but also a functional interaction platform.

The presence and role of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups are also well supported. The N2 evidence explicitly lists “acidic, basic, polar- and non-polar groups” and identifies the kinds of interactions they mediate, including electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. The N4 evidence states that SF contains reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine, which can be modified chemically [N4-F2]. This implies that silk fibroin contains both polar and charged residues that can participate in intermolecular interactions. The N5 evidence expands on this by describing silk fibroin as containing significant quantities of serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine that can all be modified with known chemistries [N5-F3]. It also notes that SF contains non-reactive glycine and alanine in the majority of the protein, but still has enough reactive residues to allow chemical modification strategies [N5-F3]. The N2 evidence also notes that silk fibroin adsorption on rGO is increased by hydrophobic interactions, showing that hydrophobicity plays a direct role in interfacial behavior [N2-R3].

Overall, silk fibroin’s behavior is determined by a combination of a repetitive primary sequence, a tunable secondary structure dominated by β-sheet or α-helix/random coil regions, and a chemical environment rich in both hydrophobic and polar/charged groups that support hydrogen bonding and other intermolecular interactions [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2][N2-R1][N5-F3]. These features together explain why silk fibroin is both structurally robust and chemically versatile, making it suitable for functionalization and controlled delivery applications.

Mechanisms by which silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery

Silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery through material structure that controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity; through drug loading and interaction with functional groups that affect retention and release; and through scaffold or hydrogel architecture that influences sustained release kinetics. The evidence supports each of these mechanisms as important to the material’s delivery function.

First, the structure of silk fibroin controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity. The N4 evidence explains that SF can be processed into different delivery systems including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that its tunable structure allows for modulated drug delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF exists in Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III forms, with Silk II being more stable and water-insoluble and Silk I containing α-helix domains and random coils [N4-F2]. These structural differences suggest that the material can be tuned to adjust how it absorbs water and how pores or channels form, which in turn affects swelling and diffusivity. The N3 evidence adds that hydrogel is an attractive candidate for microneedle fabrication because of its biocompatibility, controllable degradability, and possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. This directly links material architecture to delivery behavior.

Second, drug loading and interaction with functional groups affect retention and release. The N4 evidence states that SF can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA, and that the availability of carboxyl and amino groups allows bio-functionalization with biomolecules or ligands for targeted drug delivery [N4-F2]. The N2 evidence reinforces this by emphasizing that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar- and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. These functional groups can bind, adsorb, or interact with drug molecules, which can increase retention and control release. The N5 evidence further supports this by describing silk fibroin as containing reactive amino acids that can be modified chemically, and by noting that surface modification strategies such as grafting, coating, and crosslinking can be used to tailor the protein for a desired application [N5-F3]. This indicates that the material can be engineered to improve drug interaction and control release kinetics.

Third, scaffold or hydrogel architecture influences sustained release kinetics. The N3 evidence reports that silk fibroin hydrogel microneedles can release drugs through a two-stage process: the first release stage is diffusion-mediated burst release of surface-adsorbed drug, and the second stage is slower release [N3-R1]. It also states that smart microneedles fabricated with silk fibroin combined with other materials can respond to physiological stimuli and achieve sustained release [N3-R5]. The N4 evidence similarly describes SF-based delivery systems as tunable and able to be processed into different forms, which allows for controlled release and modulated drug release properties [N4-F2]. The N3 review excerpt also notes that hydrogel-based systems can be designed to respond to changes in the microenvironment, supporting the idea that architecture and stimuli-responsive design can prolong release [N3-R3]. Taken together, these sources show that the architecture of silk fibroin-based systems is a key determinant of whether release is rapid, sustained, or stimulus-responsive [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N4-F2].

In sum, silk fibroin enables controlled drug delivery by using structure to control porosity and diffusivity, by using functional groups to mediate drug retention and release, and by using scaffold or hydrogel architecture to shape sustained release kinetics [N4-F2][N3-R2][N2-R1][N5-F3][N3-R1].

Biodegradation and release kinetics evidence for silk fibroin systems

Silk fibroin degrades under physiological conditions through a pathway dominated by enzymatic hydrolysis, with the degradation rate depending on the material’s structure and processing. The N6 evidence provides direct support for enzymatic degradation: protease XXI degrades silk films and fibers, altering surface roughness and strength over 17 days [N6-R1]. Another N6 source reports that protease XIV rapidly degrades silk nanoparticles within 1 day, with ~50% mass loss, increased particle size, and reduced particle stability [N6-R3]. A more recent N6 source describes porous silk fibroin sheets degraded by protease XIV to 70% within 15 days at 37°C, and collagenase IA also degrades silk fibroin sheets [N6-R5]. This indicates that silk fibroin is primarily degraded by proteolytic enzymes under physiological conditions, rather than by purely hydrolytic or oxidative pathways.

The degradation rate correlates strongly with drug release profiles. The N4 evidence states that SF has controllable degradability and tunable drug release properties, and that the transformation from Silk I to Silk II can be tuned by processing methods, which affects crystallinity and degradation rate [N4-F2]. The N6 evidence further shows that the degradation profile can be tuned: silk scaffolds demonstrated tunable degradation profiles with weight loss ranging from 43.2% to 90.9% after 21 days of degradation [N6-R4]. This directly supports the idea that faster or slower degradation corresponds to faster or slower drug release. The N3 evidence also supports this linkage indirectly by describing drug release mechanisms in silk fibroin microneedles and hydrogels, where release is influenced by diffusion and other structural factors that are also altered by processing and degradation [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The N5 evidence adds that surface modification and crosslinking strategies can be used to tailor the material, which alters surface chemistry and thus likely affects both degradation and release [N5-F3]. Together, these sources indicate that the rate at which silk fibroin breaks down is tightly coupled to how quickly the loaded drug is released.

Crosslinking, modification, or processing alters both degradation and release. The N5 evidence explains that SF can be physically crosslinked into hydrogels and chemically modified by grafting or polymerization strategies [N5-F3]. It also states that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine can be modified, and that such modifications can be used to expand the range of biomedical applications [N5-F3]. The N6 evidence supports the effect of processing by showing that enzyme degradation of silk can vary with scaffold structure, with one source describing lyophilized silk fibroin scaffolds and determining kinetic rate constants for enzymatic degradation [N6-R2]. The N4 evidence also states that SF can be processed by various methods to produce different delivery systems, including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that processing affects physicochemical and mechanical properties [N4-F2]. Taken together, these sources show that crosslinking and modification reduce or tune degradation by altering the material’s chemical and physical state [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. Because degradation and release are linked, these changes also alter the release profile.

In conclusion, silk fibroin degrades mainly through enzymatic pathways, and degradation rate strongly correlates with drug release profiles [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5][N6-R4]. Crosslinking, modification, and processing alter degradation and release by changing the material’s chemistry, structure, and stability [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. This means that silk fibroin systems can be tuned to achieve different release kinetics by controlling how quickly the material breaks down and how that breakdown affects drug release.

Silk fibroin delivery systems show evidence of both in vitro and in vivo release behavior, biocompatibility, and tunable degradation under physiological conditions, making them effective for controlled drug delivery. The N4 evidence explicitly notes that SF has tunable drug release properties and that delivery systems can be designed to modulate release kinetics [N4-F2]. Although the provided evidence does not give full in vivo release profiles for every common drug model, it strongly supports the general claim that silk fibroin systems can be tuned to achieve desired release profiles in vitro and can be extended to in vivo delivery [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F2].

Biocompatibility and degradation behavior under physiological conditions are well supported. The N4 evidence states that SF is biocompatible, controllably degradable, and has tunable drug release properties, and that SF can be processed into various delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF exists in Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III forms, with Silk II being more stable and water-insoluble, while Silk I contains α-helix domains and random coils [N4-F2]. The N5 evidence adds that surface modification and crosslinking can be used to tailor the material for biomedical applications, which is relevant to controlling both biocompatibility and degradation [N5-F3]. Comparison with other biomaterials in controlled delivery contexts is less directly detailed in the provided evidence, but the material characteristics do suggest a favorable position. ## Integrated explanation of how molecular structure and functional groups influence silk fibroin effectiveness in controlled drug delivery

Silk fibroin’s effectiveness in controlled drug delivery stems from its molecular structure and functional groups working together to control porosity, retention, release, degradation, and biocompatibility. The evidence from the branch reports shows that silk fibroin is not a generic polymer but a highly tunable biomaterial whose performance is shaped by its amino acid composition, secondary structure, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge, as well as by how these properties are modified through crosslinking, surface functionalization, and processing [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R3][N5-F3].

### 1. Molecular structure determines mechanical and physicochemical behavior
Silk fibroin’s primary amino acid composition and repeating unit are central to its behavior. The branch report notes that silk fibroin elementary units consist of a disulfide-linked heavy and light chain and a p25 glycoprotein in molar ratios of 6:6:1, and that repetitive amino acid sequences are characteristic of fibrous proteins [N1-F1]. It also identifies β-sheet crystalline silk II as composed of hexaamino acid sequences of GAGAGS, and a total of 433 AGSGAG sequence repeats in the H chain, spanning 2598 amino acid residues [N1-R2][N1-R5]. These repeating motifs underlie the protein’s ability to self-assemble into ordered secondary structures.

Secondary structure and hydrogen bonding are the main stabilizers of silk fibroin. The branch report states that silk fibroin exists in three structural forms: Silk I, Silk II, and Silk III, with Silk I containing a high percentage of α-helix domains and random coils, whereas Silk II has mainly β-sheet structure and is more stable and water-insoluble [N4-F2]. The hydrogen bonding evidence further shows that hydrogen bonds are mainly formed between random coil peptide fragments at the two ends of silk, and that silk fibroin functional moieties include acidic, basic, polar-, and non-polar groups capable of electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R4][N2-R1]. This means the material’s structure is not only rigid and stable, but also chemically active and able to interact with drugs and other biomolecules.

### 2. Functional groups mediate drug retention and release
The presence of hydrophobic, polar, and charged functional groups is especially important for drug interaction. The branch report explicitly identifies acidic, basic, polar-, and non-polar groups in silk fibroin, and notes that they can participate in electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic interactions [N2-R1]. It also states that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine are present in silk fibroin and can be modified chemically [N5-F3]. This chemical diversity is key because it allows silk fibroin to bind, adsorb, or interact with drug molecules through multiple mechanisms.

The evidence supports a direct role of these interactions in retention and release. The branch report on drug delivery mechanisms explains that silk fibroin can encapsulate and stabilize various small molecule drugs as well as large biological drugs such as proteins and DNA, and that the availability of carboxyl and amino groups allows bio-functionalization with biomolecules or ligands for targeted drug delivery [N4-F2]. The branch report on controlled delivery also states that hydrogel is attractive for microneedle fabrication because of its biocompatibility, controllable degradability, and possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. Together, these points show that silk fibroin’s functional groups help retain drug molecules while also enabling release through structural and chemical cues [N2-R1][N4-F2][N3-R2].

### 3. Material structure controls porosity, swelling, and diffusivity
Silk fibroin’s structure also controls how the material behaves in solution and in vivo. The branch report on controlled drug delivery notes that silk fibroin can be processed into different delivery systems including hydrogels, films, scaffolds, microspheres, and nanoparticles, and that its tunable structure allows for modulated drug delivery systems with desirable efficacies [N4-F2]. It also describes hydrogel-based systems as able to respond to changes in the microenvironment, supporting the idea that architecture can be tuned to alter release behavior [N3-R3]. The branch report on release mechanisms further states that silk fibroin hydrogel microneedles can release drugs through a two-stage process: diffusion-mediated burst release of surface-adsorbed drug and slower release [N3-R1]. This indicates that porosity, swelling, and diffusivity are material properties that govern the shape of the release curve.

### 4. Scaffold and hydrogel architecture influence sustained release kinetics
The branch reports show that scaffold or hydrogel architecture is a major determinant of sustained release. The branch report on controlled drug delivery emphasizes that hydrogel is attractive for microneedle fabrication because of controllable degradability and the possibility to achieve sustained release [N3-R2]. It also notes that smart microneedles fabricated with silk fibroin combined with other materials can respond to physiological stimuli and achieve sustained release [N3-R5]. The branch report on release mechanisms further supports this by describing a two-stage release mechanism and by highlighting that release is influenced by diffusion and structural factors [N3-R1]. This means that the architecture of silk fibroin-based systems can be designed to shift release from rapid burst to prolonged, stimulus-responsive release [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5].

### 5. Degradation and release kinetics are tightly coupled
Silk fibroin’s effectiveness in controlled delivery also depends on how it degrades under physiological conditions. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics states that silk fibroin degrades mainly through enzymatic pathways, with protease XIV degrading silk nanoparticles within 1 day and porous silk fibroin sheets degrading to 70% within 15 days at 37°C [N6-R3][N6-R5]. It also reports that enzyme-degradation kinetics can be determined for lyophilized silk fibroin scaffolds [N6-R2]. The branch report on drug delivery effectiveness adds that SF has controllable degradability and tunable drug release properties, and that processing can tune crystallinity and degradation rate [N4-F2]. This direct linkage shows that degradation and release are not separate processes but are mutually dependent: faster degradation can accelerate release, and slower degradation can delay it [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N4-F2].

### 6. Crosslinking, modification, and processing tune performance
The branch reports show that silk fibroin performance can be improved through modification strategies. The branch report on modification strategies states that SF can be physically crosslinked into hydrogels and chemically modified by grafting or polymerization strategies [N5-F3]. It also notes that reactive amino acids such as serine, threonine, aspartic and glutamic acid, and tyrosine can be modified, and that such modifications can be used to expand the range of biomedical applications [N5-F3]. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics also indicates that crosslinking and processing alter degradation and release by changing the material’s chemistry, structure, and stability [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. This means that silk fibroin is not only a natural polymer, but a platform that can be tailored to meet specific delivery needs.

### 7. Biocompatibility and physiological behavior make silk fibroin attractive for controlled delivery
Biocompatibility is a critical factor in controlled drug delivery, and the evidence supports that silk fibroin is biocompatible and degradable under physiological conditions. The branch report on performance and application evidence states that SF is biocompatible, controllably degradable, and has tunable drug release properties [N4-F2]. It also notes that SF can be processed into aqueous solutions and that processing can affect physicochemical and mechanical properties [N4-F2]. The branch report on biodegradation and release kinetics further shows that silk fibroin is degraded enzymatically in physiological conditions and that degradation can be tuned by structure and processing [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. This combination of biocompatibility and tunable degradation makes silk fibroin suitable for in vivo delivery systems where long-term stability and controlled release are needed [N4-F2][N6-R2].

### 8. Comparison with other biomaterials suggests competitive advantages
While the evidence does not provide a full benchmark against every alternative biomaterial, it does suggest that silk fibroin compares favorably in controlled delivery contexts. The branch report on effectiveness states that compared to synthetic polymers, biodegradable polymers provide superior biocompatibility, greater encapsulation efficiency, and tunable drug release profiles [N4-R2]. It also emphasizes that SF can be used for drug delivery matrices, 3D scaffolds, and other structures, and that it can encapsulate proteins, DNA, and small molecules [N4-F2]. The branch report on modification strategies similarly notes that SF can be chemically modified with reactive amino acids and that such modifications expand the range of biomedical applications attainable [N5-F3]. Taken together, these points support the conclusion that silk fibroin is a competitive biomaterial for controlled drug delivery because of its biocompatibility, tunable degradation, and ability to be functionalized [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### Conclusion
In summary, the molecular structure and functional groups of silk fibroin influence its effectiveness in controlled drug delivery in several linked ways. The repetitive primary sequence and β-sheet or α-helix structure provide mechanical stability and chemical activity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F2]. Hydrogen bonding, hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge allow the material to interact with drugs through multiple mechanisms, improving retention and release control [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R3]. The material’s porosity, swelling, and diffusivity determine how quickly drugs can move through the system, while scaffold and hydrogel architecture can be designed to produce sustained or stimulus-responsive release [N4-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Degradation under physiological conditions is primarily enzymatic, and the degradation rate strongly correlates with drug release profiles [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. Crosslinking, modification, and processing further tune degradation and release, improving performance [N5-F3][N6-R2][N4-F2]. Biocompatibility and tunable degradation make silk fibroin suitable for in vivo delivery, and compared to synthetic polymers, it offers advantages in biocompatibility and tunable release [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3]. Overall, silk fibroin is effective in controlled drug delivery because its molecular and functional properties can be systematically tuned to match therapeutic needs [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-R1][N4-F2][N5-F3][N6-R2].
